content.comment_body: Hello everyone! I've recently completed some small projects with your help and everything went smoothly. Now, I've written a program for a filter installation where, despite functioning correctly, the use of numerous function blocks has made it look quite complicated. My question is whether there’s a way to simplify that section of my program to save time on future projects and improve readability for myself and others. I see this as a good opportunity to learn something new. I've included a PDF document that explains the program further. The flushing cycle – which starts automatically via the HMI panel or when the pressure difference between the two transmitters exceeds 0.5 bar – acts by opening each valve for 5 seconds, then closing/resetting it, followed by a 10-minute pause. This process repeats for 12 valves. Once complete, the system returns to normal operation, or an error is triggered after four flush cycles if the pressure remains high. While everything works fine for now, I’d still appreciate a way to make it easier to follow. Interested in hearing your suggestions! Kind regards, [user_name]

Are you really expecting someone to read and reorganize such a complex program with limited documentation and unclear naming? Structuring this without proper explanations would be a tough task, even if offered substantial payment.

Hi! I’m not asking anyone to reorganize the entire program. I only included everything for clarity, though it's more complex than it needs to be. My main question is whether you can control a valve for 5 seconds, then reset and wait 10 minutes before moving on to the next valve, continuing this for 12 valves—without copying and pasting code for each individual valve. While the program is structured, having so much code on one page makes things look cluttered. Is there a way to define the sequence once and execute it for each valve in order, like a loop? I hope this explanation was clearer!
If repeating the same sequence for each valve manually remains the only solution, that's acceptable as long as it works. However, I was hoping there’s a simpler method.

You could implement a pulse generator, specifying both the flushing and pause durations. A counter can increment with each pulse—on reaching 12 pulses, the cycle ends. You can then assign each counter value to a corresponding valve. That’s one possible approach.
I've created an example program for three valves for you.
I hadn't considered that solution before, but it really helps me! Thank you very much, and sorry for any earlier confusion. Kind regards, [user_name]

No worries. One important tip: always create clear diagrams and provide good documentation from the beginning. Without this, others may struggle to understand your work, but after some time, you might have trouble with it yourself.

analysis.insight_summary: The user’s program for filter installation is effective but has become cluttered due to repetitive code blocks for each valve, making it difficult to maintain and scale. Another user offers a more streamlined approach using pulse generators and counters to simplify logic and enhance readability.
analysis.user_expectations: The user hopes for a clearer, more maintainable program structure that minimizes repetitive code and is easier to read and modify, both for themselves and for others.
